<article>
France's top court blocks social media ban for under-15s

PARIS (Reuters) — France's top court on Friday blocked a bill banning social media access for under-15s, saying it infringed upon freedom of expression and delivering a setback for President Emmanuel Macron, who asked his government to rewrite the legislation.

The Constitutional Council, ruling on two parliamentary referrals, found that Article 1 of the law "constitutes an infringement that is neither appropriate, necessary, nor proportionate" to the freedom of expression and communication of children under 15.

The law would have barred children younger than 15 from opening a social media account from September 1, and platforms would have had to close existing accounts within four months using age verification approved by the French privacy regulator. French lawmakers approved the ban in July, which would have made France the first European country to enact such a measure, after Australia barred under-16s from platforms including Facebook, TikTok and YouTube in December.

The council said that by prohibiting minors under 15 from accessing certain online services, the law inherently requires every person, even an adult, to prove their age before accessing them, and the legislature did not establish the conditions and limits of that proof. It also said the ban's scope was too broad, reaching collaboration tools, communication apps and social games whose risks for minors are not established.

The Elysee said Macron ordered Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu to re-work the bill to take the Constitutional Council's concerns into account. Macron is determined the reform take effect before Spring 2027, when France holds a presidential election in which he cannot run for a third term.

France's top court blocks social media ban for under-15s

PARIS (Reuters) — France's top court on Friday blocked a bill banning social media access for under-15s, saying it infringed upon freedom of expression and delivering a setback for President Emmanuel Macron, who asked his government to rewrite the legislation.

The Constitutional Council, ruling on two parliamentary referrals, found that Article 1 of the law "constitutes an infringement that is neither appropriate, necessary, nor proportionate" to the freedom of expression and communication of children under 15.

The law would have barred children younger than 15 from opening a social media account from September 1, and platforms would have had to close existing accounts within four months using age verification approved by the French privacy regulator. French lawmakers approved the ban in July, which would have made France the first European country to enact such a measure, after Australia barred under-16s from platforms including Facebook, TikTok and YouTube in December.

The council said that by prohibiting minors under 15 from accessing certain online services, the law inherently requires every person, even an adult, to prove their age before accessing them, and the legislature did not establish the conditions and limits of that proof. It also said the ban's scope was too broad, reaching collaboration tools, communication apps and social games whose risks for minors are not established.

The Elysee said Macron ordered Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu to re-work the bill to take the Constitutional Council's concerns into account. Macron is determined the reform take effect before Spring 2027, when France holds a presidential election in which he cannot run for a third term.

PARIS (Reuters) — France's top court on Friday blocked a bill banning social media access for under-15s, saying it infringed upon freedom of expression and delivering a setback for President Emmanuel Macron, who asked his government to rewrite the legislation.

The Constitutional Council, ruling on two parliamentary referrals, found that Article 1 of the law "constitutes an infringement that is neither appropriate, necessary, nor proportionate" to the freedom of expression and communication of children under 15.

The Elysee said Macron ordered Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu to re-work the bill to take the Constitutional Council's concerns into account. Macron is determined the reform take effect before Spring 2027, when France holds a presidential election in which he cannot run for a third term.

PARIS (Reuters) — France's top court on Friday blocked a bill banning social media access for under-15s, saying it infringed upon freedom of expression and delivering a setback for President Emmanuel Macron, who asked his government to rewrite the legislation.

The Constitutional Council, ruling on two parliamentary referrals, found that Article 1 of the law "constitutes an infringement that is neither appropriate, necessary, nor proportionate" to the freedom of expression and communication of children under 15.

It also said the ban's scope was too broad, reaching collaboration tools, communication apps and social games whose risks for minors are not established.

The Elysee said Macron ordered Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu to re-work the bill to take the Constitutional Council's concerns into account. Macron is determined the reform take effect before Spring 2027, when France holds a presidential election in which he cannot run for a third term.

PARIS (Reuters) — France's top court on Friday blocked a bill banning social media access for under-15s, saying it infringed upon freedom of expression and delivering a setback for President Emmanuel Macron, who asked his government to rewrite the legislation.

The Constitutional Council, ruling on two parliamentary referrals, found that Article 1 of the law "constitutes an infringement that is neither appropriate, necessary, nor proportionate" to the freedom of expression and communication of children under 15.

It also said the ban's scope was too broad, reaching collaboration tools, communication apps and social games whose risks for minors are not established.

The Elysee said Macron ordered Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu to re-work the bill to take the Constitutional Council's concerns into account. Macron is determined the reform take effect before Spring 2027, when France holds a presidential election in which he cannot run for a third term.

<article>
Lala Batters Hawaii
NASA Earth Observatory | August 18, 2026. Story by Lindsey Doermann. Images by Lauren Dauphin.

The powerful storm delivered extreme rainfall and damaging winds to the state, passing the Island of Hawaiʻi as a category 1 hurricane.

The spiraling clouds of a tropical storm are centered near the Hawaiian island of Kauaʻi. [August 16, 2026]

The spiraling clouds of a hurricane appear near the Hawaiian Islands. Its eye is just south of the Island of Hawaiʻi. [August 15, 2026]

Lala skirts south of the Island of Hawaiʻi as a category 1 hurricane in the right image, acquired by the VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) on the Suomi NPP satellite on August 15, 2026, at about 1:45 p.m. Hawaii Standard Time (23:45 Universal Time). The storm decreased in intensity while tracking northwest and was a tropical storm when the VIIRS on the NOAA-20 satellite captured the left image about 24 hours later.

The Island of Hawaiʻi narrowly avoided a direct landfall by Hurricane Lala in mid-August 2026. The storm nonetheless delivered serious damage as it passed just south of the island on August 15 (above, right) as a category 1 storm on the Saffir-Simpson wind scale.

Lala brought rainfall totals exceeding 20 inches (50 centimeters) to parts of the island, causing flash flooding and ongoing mudflow risks. The highest rainfall total for the storm, 43.55 inches (110.6 centimeters) as of the morning of August 17, was recorded at Laupāhoehoe, on the coast northwest of Hilo. Lala downed trees, damaged bridges, and knocked homes off their foundations. Coastal areas were pummeled by large waves, while the summit of Mauna Kea, over 13,000 feet (4,000 meters) above sea level, experienced blizzard conditions.

By early afternoon on August 16, when the other image (left) was acquired, the storm had tracked northwest, roughly parallel to the island chain, and was southwest of Kauaʻi. Lala had decreased in intensity to a tropical storm, with sustained winds of 65 miles (105 kilometers) per hour, according to the National Hurricane Center.

While the Island of Hawaiʻi took the brunt of the storm, other islands also saw destructive effects. Strong winds caused widespread power outages, with more than 220,000 customers statewide without power as of the afternoon of August 16, according to news reports. Across the islands, wind and rain damaged infrastructure, and floodwaters and debris rendered roads impassable.

It has been an active tropical cyclone season in the Eastern Pacific so far in 2026, meteorologists note, consistent with what scientists expect during an El Niño, which has been underway as of mid-June. Warm water in the equatorial Pacific, the hallmark of El Niño, and the moisture and energy it transfers to the atmosphere help fuel nascent tropical storms. Lack of wind shear, another typical El Niño pattern in this region, also encourages tropical storms to develop and strengthen. The Atlantic hurricane season, in contrast, has been relatively calm, as greater wind shear over the Atlantic Ocean and Caribbean Sea during an El Niño inhibits hurricane formation by dissipating the upward motion of heat.

NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin, using VIIRS data from NASA EOSDIS LANCE, GIBS/Worldview, and the Joint Polar Satellite System (JPSS).

Lala Batters Hawaii
NASA Earth Observatory | August 18, 2026. Story by Lindsey Doermann. Images by Lauren Dauphin.

The powerful storm delivered extreme rainfall and damaging winds to the state, passing the Island of Hawaiʻi as a category 1 hurricane.

The spiraling clouds of a tropical storm are centered near the Hawaiian island of Kauaʻi. [August 16, 2026]

The spiraling clouds of a hurricane appear near the Hawaiian Islands. Its eye is just south of the Island of Hawaiʻi. [August 15, 2026]

Lala skirts south of the Island of Hawaiʻi as a category 1 hurricane in the right image, acquired by the VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) on the Suomi NPP satellite on August 15, 2026, at about 1:45 p.m. Hawaii Standard Time (23:45 Universal Time). The storm decreased in intensity while tracking northwest and was a tropical storm when the VIIRS on the NOAA-20 satellite captured the left image about 24 hours later.

The Island of Hawaiʻi narrowly avoided a direct landfall by Hurricane Lala in mid-August 2026. The storm nonetheless delivered serious damage as it passed just south of the island on August 15 (above, right) as a category 1 storm on the Saffir-Simpson wind scale.

Lala brought rainfall totals exceeding 20 inches (50 centimeters) to parts of the island, causing flash flooding and ongoing mudflow risks. The highest rainfall total for the storm, 43.55 inches (110.6 centimeters) as of the morning of August 17, was recorded at Laupāhoehoe, on the coast northwest of Hilo. Lala downed trees, damaged bridges, and knocked homes off their foundations. Coastal areas were pummeled by large waves, while the summit of Mauna Kea, over 13,000 feet (4,000 meters) above sea level, experienced blizzard conditions.

By early afternoon on August 16, when the other image (left) was acquired, the storm had tracked northwest, roughly parallel to the island chain, and was southwest of Kauaʻi. Lala had decreased in intensity to a tropical storm, with sustained winds of 65 miles (105 kilometers) per hour, according to the National Hurricane Center.

While the Island of Hawaiʻi took the brunt of the storm, other islands also saw destructive effects. Strong winds caused widespread power outages, with more than 220,000 customers statewide without power as of the afternoon of August 16, according to news reports. Across the islands, wind and rain damaged infrastructure, and floodwaters and debris rendered roads impassable.

It has been an active tropical cyclone season in the Eastern Pacific so far in 2026, meteorologists note, consistent with what scientists expect during an El Niño, which has been underway as of mid-June. Warm water in the equatorial Pacific, the hallmark of El Niño, and the moisture and energy it transfers to the atmosphere help fuel nascent tropical storms. Lack of wind shear, another typical El Niño pattern in this region, also encourages tropical storms to develop and strengthen. The Atlantic hurricane season, in contrast, has been relatively calm, as greater wind shear over the Atlantic Ocean and Caribbean Sea during an El Niño inhibits hurricane formation by dissipating the upward motion of heat.

NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin, using VIIRS data from NASA EOSDIS LANCE, GIBS/Worldview, and the Joint Polar Satellite System (JPSS).

The Island of Hawaiʻi narrowly avoided a direct landfall by Hurricane Lala in mid-August 2026. The storm nonetheless delivered serious damage as it passed just south of the island on August 15 (above, right) as a category 1 storm on the Saffir-Simpson wind scale.

Lala Batters Hawaii
NASA Earth Observatory | August 18, 2026. Story by Lindsey Doermann. Images by Lauren Dauphin.

The Island of Hawaiʻi narrowly avoided a direct landfall by Hurricane Lala in mid-August 2026. The storm nonetheless delivered serious damage as it passed just south of the island on August 15 (above, right) as a category 1 storm on the Saffir-Simpson wind scale.

Lala brought rainfall totals exceeding 20 inches (50 centimeters) to parts of the island, causing flash flooding and ongoing mudflow risks. Lala had decreased in intensity to a tropical storm, with sustained winds of 65 miles (105 kilometers) per hour, according to the National Hurricane Center.

While the Island of Hawaiʻi took the brunt of the storm, other islands also saw destructive effects. Strong winds caused widespread power outages, with more than 220,000 customers statewide without power as of the afternoon of August 16, according to news reports. Across the islands, wind and rain damaged infrastructure, and floodwaters and debris rendered roads impassable.

It has been an active tropical cyclone season in the Eastern Pacific so far in 2026, meteorologists note, consistent with what scientists expect during an El Niño, which has been underway as of mid-June. Warm water in the equatorial Pacific, the hallmark of El Niño, and the moisture and energy it transfers to the atmosphere help fuel nascent tropical storms. Lack of wind shear, another typical El Niño pattern in this region, also encourages tropical storms to develop and strengthen. The Atlantic hurricane season, in contrast, has been relatively calm, as greater wind shear over the Atlantic Ocean and Caribbean Sea during an El Niño inhibits hurricane formation by dissipating the upward motion of heat.

Lala Batters Hawaii
NASA Earth Observatory | August 18, 2026. Story by Lindsey Doermann. Images by Lauren Dauphin.

The powerful storm delivered extreme rainfall and damaging winds to the state, passing the Island of Hawaiʻi as a category 1 hurricane.

The spiraling clouds of a tropical storm are centered near the Hawaiian island of Kauaʻi. [August 16, 2026]

The spiraling clouds of a hurricane appear near the Hawaiian Islands. Its eye is just south of the Island of Hawaiʻi. [August 15, 2026]

Lala skirts south of the Island of Hawaiʻi as a category 1 hurricane in the right image, acquired by the VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) on the Suomi NPP satellite on August 15, 2026, at about 1:45 p.m. Hawaii Standard Time (23:45 Universal Time). The storm decreased in intensity while tracking northwest and was a tropical storm when the VIIRS on the NOAA-20 satellite captured the left image about 24 hours later.

The Island of Hawaiʻi narrowly avoided a direct landfall by Hurricane Lala in mid-August 2026. The storm nonetheless delivered serious damage as it passed just south of the island on August 15 (above, right) as a category 1 storm on the Saffir-Simpson wind scale.

Lala brought rainfall totals exceeding 20 inches (50 centimeters) to parts of the island, causing flash flooding and ongoing mudflow risks. The highest rainfall total for the storm, 43.55 inches (110.6 centimeters) as of the morning of August 17, was recorded at Laupāhoehoe, on the coast northwest of Hilo. Lala downed trees, damaged bridges, and knocked homes off their foundations. Coastal areas were pummeled by large waves, while the summit of Mauna Kea, over 13,000 feet (4,000 meters) above sea level, experienced blizzard conditions.

By early afternoon on August 16, when the other image (left) was acquired, the storm had tracked northwest, roughly parallel to the island chain, and was southwest of Kauaʻi. Lala had decreased in intensity to a tropical storm, with sustained winds of 65 miles (105 kilometers) per hour, according to the National Hurricane Center.

While the Island of Hawaiʻi took the brunt of the storm, other islands also saw destructive effects. Strong winds caused widespread power outages, with more than 220,000 customers statewide without power as of the afternoon of August 16, according to news reports. Across the islands, wind and rain damaged infrastructure, and floodwaters and debris rendered roads impassable.

It has been an active tropical cyclone season in the Eastern Pacific so far in 2026, meteorologists note, consistent with what scientists expect during an El Niño, which has been underway as of mid-June. Warm water in the equatorial Pacific, the hallmark of El Niño, and the moisture and energy it transfers to the atmosphere help fuel nascent tropical storms. Lack of wind shear, another typical El Niño pattern in this region, also encourages tropical storms to develop and strengthen. The Atlantic hurricane season, in contrast, has been relatively calm, as greater wind shear over the Atlantic Ocean and Caribbean Sea during an El Niño inhibits hurricane formation by dissipating the upward motion of heat.

NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin, using VIIRS data from NASA EOSDIS LANCE, GIBS/Worldview, and the Joint Polar Satellite System (JPSS).

Lala Batters Hawaii
NASA Earth Observatory | August 18, 2026. Story by Lindsey Doermann. Images by Lauren Dauphin.

The powerful storm delivered extreme rainfall and damaging winds to the state, passing the Island of Hawaiʻi as a category 1 hurricane.

The spiraling clouds of a tropical storm are centered near the Hawaiian island of Kauaʻi. [August 16, 2026]

The spiraling clouds of a hurricane appear near the Hawaiian Islands. Its eye is just south of the Island of Hawaiʻi. [August 15, 2026]

Lala skirts south of the Island of Hawaiʻi as a category 1 hurricane in the right image, acquired by the VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) on the Suomi NPP satellite on August 15, 2026, at about 1:45 p.m. Hawaii Standard Time (23:45 Universal Time). The storm decreased in intensity while tracking northwest and was a tropical storm when the VIIRS on the NOAA-20 satellite captured the left image about 24 hours later.

The Island of Hawaiʻi narrowly avoided a direct landfall by Hurricane Lala in mid-August 2026. The storm nonetheless delivered serious damage as it passed just south of the island on August 15 (above, right) as a category 1 storm on the Saffir-Simpson wind scale.

Lala brought rainfall totals exceeding 20 inches (50 centimeters) to parts of the island, causing flash flooding and ongoing mudflow risks. The highest rainfall total for the storm, 43.55 inches (110.6 centimeters) as of the morning of August 17, was recorded at Laupāhoehoe, on the coast northwest of Hilo. Lala downed trees, damaged bridges, and knocked homes off their foundations. Coastal areas were pummeled by large waves, while the summit of Mauna Kea, over 13,000 feet (4,000 meters) above sea level, experienced blizzard conditions.

By early afternoon on August 16, when the other image (left) was acquired, the storm had tracked northwest, roughly parallel to the island chain, and was southwest of Kauaʻi. Lala had decreased in intensity to a tropical storm, with sustained winds of 65 miles (105 kilometers) per hour, according to the National Hurricane Center.

While the Island of Hawaiʻi took the brunt of the storm, other islands also saw destructive effects. Strong winds caused widespread power outages, with more than 220,000 customers statewide without power as of the afternoon of August 16, according to news reports. Across the islands, wind and rain damaged infrastructure, and floodwaters and debris rendered roads impassable.

It has been an active tropical cyclone season in the Eastern Pacific so far in 2026, meteorologists note, consistent with what scientists expect during an El Niño, which has been underway as of mid-June. Warm water in the equatorial Pacific, the hallmark of El Niño, and the moisture and energy it transfers to the atmosphere help fuel nascent tropical storms. Lack of wind shear, another typical El Niño pattern in this region, also encourages tropical storms to develop and strengthen. The Atlantic hurricane season, in contrast, has been relatively calm, as greater wind shear over the Atlantic Ocean and Caribbean Sea during an El Niño inhibits hurricane formation by dissipating the upward motion of heat.

The powerful storm delivered extreme rainfall and damaging winds to the state, passing the Island of Hawaiʻi as a category 1 hurricane.

The spiraling clouds of a tropical storm are centered near the Hawaiian island of Kauaʻi. [August 16, 2026]

The spiraling clouds of a hurricane appear near the Hawaiian Islands. Its eye is just south of the Island of Hawaiʻi. [August 15, 2026]

Lala skirts south of the Island of Hawaiʻi as a category 1 hurricane in the right image, acquired by the VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) on the Suomi NPP satellite on August 15, 2026, at about 1:45 p.m. Hawaii Standard Time (23:45 Universal Time). The storm decreased in intensity while tracking northwest and was a tropical storm when the VIIRS on the NOAA-20 satellite captured the left image about 24 hours later.

The Island of Hawaiʻi narrowly avoided a direct landfall by Hurricane Lala in mid-August 2026. The storm nonetheless delivered serious damage as it passed just south of the island on August 15 (above, right) as a category 1 storm on the Saffir-Simpson wind scale.

Lala brought rainfall totals exceeding 20 inches (50 centimeters) to parts of the island, causing flash flooding and ongoing mudflow risks. The highest rainfall total for the storm, 43.55 inches (110.6 centimeters) as of the morning of August 17, was recorded at Laupāhoehoe, on the coast northwest of Hilo. Lala downed trees, damaged bridges, and knocked homes off their foundations. Coastal areas were pummeled by large waves, while the summit of Mauna Kea, over 13,000 feet (4,000 meters) above sea level, experienced blizzard conditions.

By early afternoon on August 16, when the other image (left) was acquired, the storm had tracked northwest, roughly parallel to the island chain, and was southwest of Kauaʻi. Lala had decreased in intensity to a tropical storm, with sustained winds of 65 miles (105 kilometers) per hour, according to the National Hurricane Center.

While the Island of Hawaiʻi took the brunt of the storm, other islands also saw destructive effects. Strong winds caused widespread power outages, with more than 220,000 customers statewide without power as of the afternoon of August 16, according to news reports. Across the islands, wind and rain damaged infrastructure, and floodwaters and debris rendered roads impassable.

It has been an active tropical cyclone season in the Eastern Pacific so far in 2026, meteorologists note, consistent with what scientists expect during an El Niño, which has been underway as of mid-June. Warm water in the equatorial Pacific, the hallmark of El Niño, and the moisture and energy it transfers to the atmosphere help fuel nascent tropical storms. Lack of wind shear, another typical El Niño pattern in this region, also encourages tropical storms to develop and strengthen. The Atlantic hurricane season, in contrast, has been relatively calm, as greater wind shear over the Atlantic Ocean and Caribbean Sea during an El Niño inhibits hurricane formation by dissipating the upward motion of heat.

NASA Earth Observatory | August 18, 2026. Story by Lindsey Doermann. Images by Lauren Dauphin.

The powerful storm delivered extreme rainfall and damaging winds to the state, passing the Island of Hawaiʻi as a category 1 hurricane.

The storm decreased in intensity while tracking northwest and was a tropical storm when the VIIRS on the NOAA-20 satellite captured the left image about 24 hours later.

The Island of Hawaiʻi narrowly avoided a direct landfall by Hurricane Lala in mid-August 2026. The storm nonetheless delivered serious damage as it passed just south of the island on August 15 (above, right) as a category 1 storm on the Saffir-Simpson wind scale.

Lala brought rainfall totals exceeding 20 inches (50 centimeters) to parts of the island, causing flash flooding and ongoing mudflow risks. The highest rainfall total for the storm, 43.55 inches (110.6 centimeters) as of the morning of August 17, was recorded at Laupāhoehoe, on the coast northwest of Hilo. Lala downed trees, damaged bridges, and knocked homes off their foundations. Coastal areas were pummeled by large waves, while the summit of Mauna Kea, over 13,000 feet (4,000 meters) above sea level, experienced blizzard conditions.

By early afternoon on August 16, when the other image (left) was acquired, the storm had tracked northwest, roughly parallel to the island chain, and was southwest of Kauaʻi. Lala had decreased in intensity to a tropical storm, with sustained winds of 65 miles (105 kilometers) per hour, according to the National Hurricane Center.

While the Island of Hawaiʻi took the brunt of the storm, other islands also saw destructive effects. Strong winds caused widespread power outages, with more than 220,000 customers statewide without power as of the afternoon of August 16, according to news reports. Across the islands, wind and rain damaged infrastructure, and floodwaters and debris rendered roads impassable.

It has been an active tropical cyclone season in the Eastern Pacific so far in 2026, meteorologists note, consistent with what scientists expect during an El Niño, which has been underway as of mid-June. Warm water in the equatorial Pacific, the hallmark of El Niño, and the moisture and energy it transfers to the atmosphere help fuel nascent tropical storms. Lack of wind shear, another typical El Niño pattern in this region, also encourages tropical storms to develop and strengthen. The Atlantic hurricane season, in contrast, has been relatively calm, as greater wind shear over the Atlantic Ocean and Caribbean Sea during an El Niño inhibits hurricane formation by dissipating the upward motion of heat.

Lala Batters Hawaii
NASA Earth Observatory | August 18, 2026. Story by Lindsey Doermann. Images by Lauren Dauphin.

The powerful storm delivered extreme rainfall and damaging winds to the state, passing the Island of Hawaiʻi as a category 1 hurricane.

The spiraling clouds of a tropical storm are centered near the Hawaiian island of Kauaʻi. [August 16, 2026]

The spiraling clouds of a hurricane appear near the Hawaiian Islands. Its eye is just south of the Island of Hawaiʻi. [August 15, 2026]

Lala skirts south of the Island of Hawaiʻi as a category 1 hurricane in the right image, acquired by the VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) on the Suomi NPP satellite on August 15, 2026, at about 1:45 p.m. Hawaii Standard Time (23:45 Universal Time). The storm decreased in intensity while tracking northwest and was a tropical storm when the VIIRS on the NOAA-20 satellite captured the left image about 24 hours later.

The Island of Hawaiʻi narrowly avoided a direct landfall by Hurricane Lala in mid-August 2026. The storm nonetheless delivered serious damage as it passed just south of the island on August 15 (above, right) as a category 1 storm on the Saffir-Simpson wind scale.

Lala brought rainfall totals exceeding 20 inches (50 centimeters) to parts of the island, causing flash flooding and ongoing mudflow risks. The highest rainfall total for the storm, 43.55 inches (110.6 centimeters) as of the morning of August 17, was recorded at Laupāhoehoe, on the coast northwest of Hilo. Lala downed trees, damaged bridges, and knocked homes off their foundations. Coastal areas were pummeled by large waves, while the summit of Mauna Kea, over 13,000 feet (4,000 meters) above sea level, experienced blizzard conditions.

By early afternoon on August 16, when the other image (left) was acquired, the storm had tracked northwest, roughly parallel to the island chain, and was southwest of Kauaʻi. Lala had decreased in intensity to a tropical storm, with sustained winds of 65 miles (105 kilometers) per hour, according to the National Hurricane Center.

While the Island of Hawaiʻi took the brunt of the storm, other islands also saw destructive effects. Strong winds caused widespread power outages, with more than 220,000 customers statewide without power as of the afternoon of August 16, according to news reports. Across the islands, wind and rain damaged infrastructure, and floodwaters and debris rendered roads impassable.

It has been an active tropical cyclone season in the Eastern Pacific so far in 2026, meteorologists note, consistent with what scientists expect during an El Niño, which has been underway as of mid-June. Warm water in the equatorial Pacific, the hallmark of El Niño, and the moisture and energy it transfers to the atmosphere help fuel nascent tropical storms. Lack of wind shear, another typical El Niño pattern in this region, also encourages tropical storms to develop and strengthen. The Atlantic hurricane season, in contrast, has been relatively calm, as greater wind shear over the Atlantic Ocean and Caribbean Sea during an El Niño inhibits hurricane formation by dissipating the upward motion of heat.

NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin, using VIIRS data from NASA EOSDIS LANCE, GIBS/Worldview, and the Joint Polar Satellite System (JPSS).

LAS VEGAS (AP) — The trial of Duane "Keffe D" Davis, the only person ever charged in the 1996 murder of rapper Tupac Shakur, began Monday at the Clark County District Court Regional Justice Center in Las Vegas, 30 years after one of America's most high-profile unsolved killings.

Davis, 63, the former leader of the South Side Compton Crips, has pleaded not guilty to one count of murder with a deadly weapon and could face life in prison if convicted.

"Let's be clear, Duane Davis did not pull the trigger. But he did plan the shooting in retaliation for the beating of his nephew," Chief Deputy District Attorney Binu Palal told jurors in his opening statement. "Remarkably, you will learn that from Duane Davis himself."

Prosecutors allege Davis was the "shot-caller" who conceived the plan to exact revenge on Shakur and on Death Row Records CEO Suge Knight after Shakur and his entourage beat Davis's nephew, Orlando Anderson, outside the MGM Grand hours before the September 7, 1996, drive-by. Shakur was shot multiple times in a black BMW that Knight was driving; Knight was grazed in the head. Shakur died six days later.

The case rests heavily on Davis's own statements over two decades: a confidential 1998 interview with the FBI, a 2008 interview with Los Angeles police detectives who were investigating the killing of rapper Biggie Smalls, a 2009 interview with Las Vegas police, and a 2019 memoir he co-authored, Compton Street Legend. In the 2008 interview, Davis said he passed a gun to the back seat of the car, and that his nephew Anderson fired.

Defense attorney Michael Sanft has attacked his own client's credibility, calling the years of statements and the memoir fiction. "They are telling you, they are representing as fact, when it's really fiction," Sanft told jurors.

On the second day of the trial, jurors were shown photos of Shakur's body and the casings recovered at the scene, and a forensic pathologist testified that a bullet entered Shakur's chest near his armpit and passed through his lung.

James "Mob James" McDonald, a former member of Shakur's entourage, took the stand. Knight, who is on the prosecution's witness list, has said he wants no part in the trial.

The prosecution is expected to call between 35 and 45 witnesses, and the trial is expected to last up to six weeks.

James "Mob James" McDonald, a former member of Shakur's entourage, took the stand. Knight, who is on the prosecution's witness list, has said he wants no part in the trial.

The case rests heavily on Davis's own statements over two decades: a confidential 1998 interview with the FBI, a 2008 interview with Los Angeles police detectives who were investigating the killing of rapper Biggie Smalls, a 2009 interview with Las Vegas police, and a 2019 memoir he co-authored, Compton Street Legend. James "Mob James" McDonald, a former member of Shakur's entourage, took the stand. Knight, who is on the prosecution's witness list, has said he wants no part in the trial.

LAS VEGAS (AP) — The trial of Duane "Keffe D" Davis, the only person ever charged in the 1996 murder of rapper Tupac Shakur, began Monday at the Clark County District Court Regional Justice Center in Las Vegas, 30 years after one of America's most high-profile unsolved killings.

Davis, 63, the former leader of the South Side Compton Crips, has pleaded not guilty to one count of murder with a deadly weapon and could face life in prison if convicted.

"Let's be clear, Duane Davis did not pull the trigger. But he did plan the shooting in retaliation for the beating of his nephew," Chief Deputy District Attorney Binu Palal told jurors in his opening statement. "Remarkably, you will learn that from Duane Davis himself."

Prosecutors allege Davis was the "shot-caller" who conceived the plan to exact revenge on Shakur and on Death Row Records CEO Suge Knight after Shakur and his entourage beat Davis's nephew, Orlando Anderson, outside the MGM Grand hours before the September 7, 1996, drive-by. Shakur was shot multiple times in a black BMW that Knight was driving; Knight was grazed in the head. Shakur died six days later.

The case rests heavily on Davis's own statements over two decades: a confidential 1998 interview with the FBI, a 2008 interview with Los Angeles police detectives who were investigating the killing of rapper Biggie Smalls, a 2009 interview with Las Vegas police, and a 2019 memoir he co-authored, Compton Street Legend. In the 2008 interview, Davis said he passed a gun to the back seat of the car, and that his nephew Anderson fired.

Defense attorney Michael Sanft has attacked his own client's credibility, calling the years of statements and the memoir fiction. "They are telling you, they are representing as fact, when it's really fiction," Sanft told jurors.

On the second day of the trial, jurors were shown photos of Shakur's body and the casings recovered at the scene, and a forensic pathologist testified that a bullet entered Shakur's chest near his armpit and passed through his lung.

James "Mob James" McDonald, a former member of Shakur's entourage, took the stand. Knight, who is on the prosecution's witness list, has said he wants no part in the trial.

The prosecution is expected to call between 35 and 45 witnesses, and the trial is expected to last up to six weeks.

<article>
Tupac Shakur murder trial: prosecution builds case on Davis's own words

LAS VEGAS (AP) — The trial of Duane "Keffe D" Davis, the only person ever charged in the 1996 murder of rapper Tupac Shakur, began Monday at the Clark County District Court Regional Justice Center in Las Vegas, 30 years after one of America's most high-profile unsolved killings.

Davis, 63, the former leader of the South Side Compton Crips, has pleaded not guilty to one count of murder with a deadly weapon and could face life in prison if convicted.

"Let's be clear, Duane Davis did not pull the trigger. But he did plan the shooting in retaliation for the beating of his nephew," Chief Deputy District Attorney Binu Palal told jurors in his opening statement. "Remarkably, you will learn that from Duane Davis himself."

Prosecutors allege Davis was the "shot-caller" who conceived the plan to exact revenge on Shakur and on Death Row Records CEO Suge Knight after Shakur and his entourage beat Davis's nephew, Orlando Anderson, outside the MGM Grand hours before the September 7, 1996, drive-by. Shakur was shot multiple times in a black BMW that Knight was driving; Knight was grazed in the head. Shakur died six days later.

The case rests heavily on Davis's own statements over two decades: a confidential 1998 interview with the FBI, a 2008 interview with Los Angeles police detectives who were investigating the killing of rapper Biggie Smalls, a 2009 interview with Las Vegas police, and a 2019 memoir he co-authored, Compton Street Legend. In the 2008 interview, Davis said he passed a gun to the back seat of the car, and that his nephew Anderson fired.

Defense attorney Michael Sanft has attacked his own client's credibility, calling the years of statements and the memoir fiction. "They are telling you, they are representing as fact, when it's really fiction," Sanft told jurors.

On the second day of the trial, jurors were shown photos of Shakur's body and the casings recovered at the scene, and a forensic pathologist testified that a bullet entered Shakur's chest near his armpit and passed through his lung.

James "Mob James" McDonald, a former member of Shakur's entourage, took the stand. Knight, who is on the prosecution's witness list, has said he wants no part in the trial.

The prosecution is expected to call between 35 and 45 witnesses, and the trial is expected to last up to six weeks.

<article>
Tupac Shakur murder trial: prosecution builds case on Davis's own words

LAS VEGAS (AP) — The trial of Duane "Keffe D" Davis, the only person ever charged in the 1996 murder of rapper Tupac Shakur, began Monday at the Clark County District Court Regional Justice Center in Las Vegas, 30 years after one of America's most high-profile unsolved killings.

Davis, 63, the former leader of the South Side Compton Crips, has pleaded not guilty to one count of murder with a deadly weapon and could face life in prison if convicted.

"Let's be clear, Duane Davis did not pull the trigger. But he did plan the shooting in retaliation for the beating of his nephew," Chief Deputy District Attorney Binu Palal told jurors in his opening statement. "Remarkably, you will learn that from Duane Davis himself."

Prosecutors allege Davis was the "shot-caller" who conceived the plan to exact revenge on Shakur and on Death Row Records CEO Suge Knight after Shakur and his entourage beat Davis's nephew, Orlando Anderson, outside the MGM Grand hours before the September 7, 1996, drive-by. Shakur was shot multiple times in a black BMW that Knight was driving; Knight was grazed in the head. Shakur died six days later.

The case rests heavily on Davis's own statements over two decades: a confidential 1998 interview with the FBI, a 2008 interview with Los Angeles police detectives who were investigating the killing of rapper Biggie Smalls, a 2009 interview with Las Vegas police, and a 2019 memoir he co-authored, Compton Street Legend. In the 2008 interview, Davis said he passed a gun to the back seat of the car, and that his nephew Anderson fired.

Defense attorney Michael Sanft has attacked his own client's credibility, calling the years of statements and the memoir fiction. "They are telling you, they are representing as fact, when it's really fiction," Sanft told jurors.

On the second day of the trial, jurors were shown photos of Shakur's body and the casings recovered at the scene, and a forensic pathologist testified that a bullet entered Shakur's chest near his armpit and passed through his lung.

James "Mob James" McDonald, a former member of Shakur's entourage, took the stand. Knight, who is on the prosecution's witness list, has said he wants no part in the trial.

The prosecution is expected to call between 35 and 45 witnesses, and the trial is expected to last up to six weeks.
</article>

James "Mob James" McDonald, a former member of Shakur's entourage, took the stand. Knight, who is on the prosecution's witness list, has said he wants no part in the trial.

<article>
Tupac Shakur murder trial: prosecution builds case on Davis's own words

LAS VEGAS (AP) — The trial of Duane "Keffe D" Davis, the only person ever charged in the 1996 murder of rapper Tupac Shakur, began Monday at the Clark County District Court Regional Justice Center in Las Vegas, 30 years after one of America's most high-profile unsolved killings.

Davis, 63, the former leader of the South Side Compton Crips, has pleaded not guilty to one count of murder with a deadly weapon and could face life in prison if convicted.

"Let's be clear, Duane Davis did not pull the trigger. But he did plan the shooting in retaliation for the beating of his nephew," Chief Deputy District Attorney Binu Palal told jurors in his opening statement. "Remarkably, you will learn that from Duane Davis himself."

Prosecutors allege Davis was the "shot-caller" who conceived the plan to exact revenge on Shakur and on Death Row Records CEO Suge Knight after Shakur and his entourage beat Davis's nephew, Orlando Anderson, outside the MGM Grand hours before the September 7, 1996, drive-by. Shakur was shot multiple times in a black BMW that Knight was driving; Knight was grazed in the head. Shakur died six days later.

The case rests heavily on Davis's own statements over two decades: a confidential 1998 interview with the FBI, a 2008 interview with Los Angeles police detectives who were investigating the killing of rapper Biggie Smalls, a 2009 interview with Las Vegas police, and a 2019 memoir he co-authored, Compton Street Legend. In the 2008 interview, Davis said he passed a gun to the back seat of the car, and that his nephew Anderson fired.

Defense attorney Michael Sanft has attacked his own client's credibility, calling the years of statements and the memoir fiction. "They are telling you, they are representing as fact, when it's really fiction," Sanft told jurors.

On the second day of the trial, jurors were shown photos of Shakur's body and the casings recovered at the scene, and a forensic pathologist testified that a bullet entered Shakur's chest near his armpit and passed through his lung.

James "Mob James" McDonald, a former member of Shakur's entourage, took the stand. Knight, who is on the prosecution's witness list, has said he wants no part in the trial.

The prosecution is expected to call between 35 and 45 witnesses, and the trial is expected to last up to six weeks.
</article>

Davis, 63, the former leader of the South Side Compton Crips, has pleaded not guilty to one count of murder with a deadly weapon and could face life in prison if convicted.

"Let's be clear, Duane Davis did not pull the trigger. But he did plan the shooting in retaliation for the beating of his nephew," Chief Deputy District Attorney Binu Palal told jurors in his opening statement. "Remarkably, you will learn that from Duane Davis himself."

Prosecutors allege Davis was the "shot-caller" who conceived the plan to exact revenge on Shakur and on Death Row Records CEO Suge Knight after Shakur and his entourage beat Davis's nephew, Orlando Anderson, outside the MGM Grand hours before the September 7, 1996, drive-by. Shakur was shot multiple times in a black BMW that Knight was driving; Knight was grazed in the head. Shakur died six days later.

The case rests heavily on Davis's own statements over two decades: a confidential 1998 interview with the FBI, a 2008 interview with Los Angeles police detectives who were investigating the killing of rapper Biggie Smalls, a 2009 interview with Las Vegas police, and a 2019 memoir he co-authored, Compton Street Legend. In the 2008 interview, Davis said he passed a gun to the back seat of the car, and that his nephew Anderson fired.

James "Mob James" McDonald, a former member of Shakur's entourage, took the stand. Knight, who is on the prosecution's witness list, has said he wants no part in the trial.

The prosecution is expected to call between 35 and 45 witnesses, and the trial is expected to last up to six weeks.

Davis, 63, the former leader of the South Side Compton Crips, has pleaded not guilty to one count of murder with a deadly weapon and could face life in prison if convicted.

James "Mob James" McDonald, a former member of Shakur's entourage, took the stand. Knight, who is on the prosecution's witness list, has said he wants no part in the trial.

The prosecution is expected to call between 35 and 45 witnesses, and the trial is expected to last up to six weeks.

Tupac Shakur murder trial: prosecution builds case on Davis's own words

LAS VEGAS (AP) — The trial of Duane "Keffe D" Davis, the only person ever charged in the 1996 murder of rapper Tupac Shakur, began Monday at the Clark County District Court Regional Justice Center in Las Vegas, 30 years after one of America's most high-profile unsolved killings.

Davis, 63, the former leader of the South Side Compton Crips, has pleaded not guilty to one count of murder with a deadly weapon and could face life in prison if convicted.

"Let's be clear, Duane Davis did not pull the trigger. But he did plan the shooting in retaliation for the beating of his nephew," Chief Deputy District Attorney Binu Palal told jurors in his opening statement. "Remarkably, you will learn that from Duane Davis himself."

Prosecutors allege Davis was the "shot-caller" who conceived the plan to exact revenge on Shakur and on Death Row Records CEO Suge Knight after Shakur and his entourage beat Davis's nephew, Orlando Anderson, outside the MGM Grand hours before the September 7, 1996, drive-by. Shakur was shot multiple times in a black BMW that Knight was driving; Knight was grazed in the head. Shakur died six days later.

The case rests heavily on Davis's own statements over two decades: a confidential 1998 interview with the FBI, a 2008 interview with Los Angeles police detectives who were investigating the killing of rapper Biggie Smalls, a 2009 interview with Las Vegas police, and a 2019 memoir he co-authored, Compton Street Legend. In the 2008 interview, Davis said he passed a gun to the back seat of the car, and that his nephew Anderson fired.

Defense attorney Michael Sanft has attacked his own client's credibility, calling the years of statements and the memoir fiction. "They are telling you, they are representing as fact, when it's really fiction," Sanft told jurors.

On the second day of the trial, jurors were shown photos of Shakur's body and the casings recovered at the scene, and a forensic pathologist testified that a bullet entered Shakur's chest near his armpit and passed through his lung.

James "Mob James" McDonald, a former member of Shakur's entourage, took the stand. Knight, who is on the prosecution's witness list, has said he wants no part in the trial.

The prosecution is expected to call between 35 and 45 witnesses, and the trial is expected to last up to six weeks.

Tiangong Ultra, developed by the Beijing Humanoid Robot Innovation Center, won its heat at the opening of the second edition of the games, held at Beijing's National Speed Skating Oval, known as the Ice Ribbon. The robot overtook Honor's Lightning near the finish after falling behind early in the race; Lightning finished in 9.47 seconds, also faster than the 9.58-second record Bolt set at the 2009 World Athletics Championships.

At the end of the dash, the robots slammed into a cushion wall and fell to the ground to stop, and footage showed them being carried off on stretchers.

Before the opening, a humanoid robot from Chinese smartphone maker Honor completed a 100-metre sprint in 9.32 seconds during a trial of the games at a peak speed of 14.5 metres per second.

At last year's first edition of the games, the best time in the event was 21.50 seconds, so the new mark marks a leap in the running speed of humanoid robots.

More than 2,000 robots from 666 teams are competing in Beijing across 51 events. The games are being held the same week as the 2026 World Robot Conference, where thousands of products are on display.

Chinese robot beats Usain Bolt's 100m world record at Beijing games

BEIJING (Reuters) — A Chinese humanoid robot ran 100 metres in 9.39 seconds in a preliminary heat at the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing on Saturday, faster than the men's world record held by Jamaican sprinting great Usain Bolt.

Tiangong Ultra, developed by the Beijing Humanoid Robot Innovation Center, won its heat at the opening of the second edition of the games, held at Beijing's National Speed Skating Oval, known as the Ice Ribbon. The robot overtook Honor's Lightning near the finish after falling behind early in the race; Lightning finished in 9.47 seconds, also faster than the 9.58-second record Bolt set at the 2009 World Athletics Championships.

At the end of the dash, the robots slammed into a cushion wall and fell to the ground to stop, and footage showed them being carried off on stretchers.

Before the opening, a humanoid robot from Chinese smartphone maker Honor completed a 100-metre sprint in 9.32 seconds during a trial of the games at a peak speed of 14.5 metres per second.

At last year's first edition of the games, the best time in the event was 21.50 seconds, so the new mark marks a leap in the running speed of humanoid robots.

More than 2,000 robots from 666 teams are competing in Beijing across 51 events. The games are being held the same week as the 2026 World Robot Conference, where thousands of products are on display.

<article>
Chinese robot beats Usain Bolt's 100m world record at Beijing games

BEIJING (Reuters) — A Chinese humanoid robot ran 100 metres in 9.39 seconds in a preliminary heat at the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing on Saturday, faster than the men's world record held by Jamaican sprinting great Usain Bolt.

Tiangong Ultra, developed by the Beijing Humanoid Robot Innovation Center, won its heat at the opening of the second edition of the games, held at Beijing's National Speed Skating Oval, known as the Ice Ribbon. The robot overtook Honor's Lightning near the finish after falling behind early in the race; Lightning finished in 9.47 seconds, also faster than the 9.58-second record Bolt set at the 2009 World Athletics Championships.

At the end of the dash, the robots slammed into a cushion wall and fell to the ground to stop, and footage showed them being carried off on stretchers.

Before the opening, a humanoid robot from Chinese smartphone maker Honor completed a 100-metre sprint in 9.32 seconds during a trial of the games at a peak speed of 14.5 metres per second.

At last year's first edition of the games, the best time in the event was 21.50 seconds, so the new mark marks a leap in the running speed of humanoid robots.

More than 2,000 robots from 666 teams are competing in Beijing across 51 events. The games are being held the same week as the 2026 World Robot Conference, where thousands of products are on display.
</article>

OTTAWA (Reuters) — Canada will impose tariffs on US goods in retaliation for the 50 percent levies that took effect just after midnight on Saturday, Prime Minister Mark Carney said, after three days of trade talks between the two neighbours collapsed.

The "dollar for dollar" tariffs on imports of US steel, dairy, household appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics will take effect on September 8, the Tuesday after Labor Day.

The new US tariffs cover roughly $20 billion of Canadian exports, about 5 percent of Canada's annual trade with the United States, and span sectors from wine to hockey equipment. They were ordered under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 and stack on top of a 10 percent levy imposed earlier this month.

President Donald Trump announced the 50 percent tariffs in an executive order on July 20, accusing Canada of "discriminatory treatment" in its trade policies. They were initially set to take effect on August 19 but Trump granted a three-day pause, saying the two countries were close to a deal.

The pause ran out without an agreement. Late on Friday, Carney said he was suspending trade negotiations and ordering Canadian negotiators back to Ottawa.

"We were not prepared to compromise Canada's sovereignty or undermine our key industries," Carney said in a 22-minute address to Canadians. "You're at war when you're attacked, and we got attacked."

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said there are no future talks planned with Canada and that Washington is moving forward with measures to respond to Canadian retaliation. The breakdown complicates the future of the USMCA free trade deal.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford, whose province is hit hardest by the tariffs, said he backed Carney's position "tariff for tariff, dollar for dollar."

US 50% tariffs on Canadian goods take effect; Carney vows retaliation

OTTAWA (Reuters) — Canada will impose tariffs on US goods in retaliation for the 50 percent levies that took effect just after midnight on Saturday, Prime Minister Mark Carney said, after three days of trade talks between the two neighbours collapsed.

The "dollar for dollar" tariffs on imports of US steel, dairy, household appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics will take effect on September 8, the Tuesday after Labor Day.

The new US tariffs cover roughly $20 billion of Canadian exports, about 5 percent of Canada's annual trade with the United States, and span sectors from wine to hockey equipment. They were ordered under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 and stack on top of a 10 percent levy imposed earlier this month.

President Donald Trump announced the 50 percent tariffs in an executive order on July 20, accusing Canada of "discriminatory treatment" in its trade policies. They were initially set to take effect on August 19 but Trump granted a three-day pause, saying the two countries were close to a deal.

The pause ran out without an agreement. Late on Friday, Carney said he was suspending trade negotiations and ordering Canadian negotiators back to Ottawa.

"We were not prepared to compromise Canada's sovereignty or undermine our key industries," Carney said in a 22-minute address to Canadians. "You're at war when you're attacked, and we got attacked."

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said there are no future talks planned with Canada and that Washington is moving forward with measures to respond to Canadian retaliation. The breakdown complicates the future of the USMCA free trade deal.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford, whose province is hit hardest by the tariffs, said he backed Carney's position "tariff for tariff, dollar for dollar."

OTTAWA (Reuters) — Canada will impose tariffs on US goods in retaliation for the 50 percent levies that took effect just after midnight on Saturday, Prime Minister Mark Carney said, after three days of trade talks between the two neighbours collapsed.

The "dollar for dollar" tariffs on imports of US steel, dairy, household appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics will take effect on September 8, the Tuesday after Labor Day.

The new US tariffs cover roughly $20 billion of Canadian exports, about 5 percent of Canada's annual trade with the United States, and span sectors from wine to hockey equipment. President Donald Trump announced the 50 percent tariffs in an executive order on July 20, accusing Canada of "discriminatory treatment" in its trade policies. They were initially set to take effect on August 19 but Trump granted a three-day pause, saying the two countries were close to a deal.

"We were not prepared to compromise Canada's sovereignty or undermine our key industries," Carney said in a 22-minute address to Canadians. "You're at war when you're attacked, and we got attacked."

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said there are no future talks planned with Canada and that Washington is moving forward with measures to respond to Canadian retaliation. The breakdown complicates the future of the USMCA free trade deal.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford, whose province is hit hardest by the tariffs, said he backed Carney's position "tariff for tariff, dollar for dollar."

OTTAWA (Reuters) — Canada will impose tariffs on US goods in retaliation for the 50 percent levies that took effect just after midnight on Saturday, Prime Minister Mark Carney said, after three days of trade talks between the two neighbours collapsed.

The "dollar for dollar" tariffs on imports of US steel, dairy, household appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics will take effect on September 8, the Tuesday after Labor Day.

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said there are no future talks planned with Canada and that Washington is moving forward with measures to respond to Canadian retaliation. The breakdown complicates the future of the USMCA free trade deal.

US 50% tariffs on Canadian goods take effect; Carney vows retaliation

OTTAWA (Reuters) — Canada will impose tariffs on US goods in retaliation for the 50 percent levies that took effect just after midnight on Saturday, Prime Minister Mark Carney said, after three days of trade talks between the two neighbours collapsed.

The "dollar for dollar" tariffs on imports of US steel, dairy, household appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics will take effect on September 8, the Tuesday after Labor Day.

The new US tariffs cover roughly $20 billion of Canadian exports, about 5 percent of Canada's annual trade with the United States, and span sectors from wine to hockey equipment. They were ordered under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 and stack on top of a 10 percent levy imposed earlier this month.

President Donald Trump announced the 50 percent tariffs in an executive order on July 20, accusing Canada of "discriminatory treatment" in its trade policies. They were initially set to take effect on August 19 but Trump granted a three-day pause, saying the two countries were close to a deal.

The pause ran out without an agreement. Late on Friday, Carney said he was suspending trade negotiations and ordering Canadian negotiators back to Ottawa.

"We were not prepared to compromise Canada's sovereignty or undermine our key industries," Carney said in a 22-minute address to Canadians. "You're at war when you're attacked, and we got attacked."

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said there are no future talks planned with Canada and that Washington is moving forward with measures to respond to Canadian retaliation. The breakdown complicates the future of the USMCA free trade deal.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford, whose province is hit hardest by the tariffs, said he backed Carney's position "tariff for tariff, dollar for dollar."

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said there are no future talks planned with Canada and that Washington is moving forward with measures to respond to Canadian retaliation. The breakdown complicates the future of the USMCA free trade deal.

The "dollar for dollar" tariffs on imports of US steel, dairy, household appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics will take effect on September 8, the Tuesday after Labor Day.

The new US tariffs cover roughly $20 billion of Canadian exports, about 5 percent of Canada's annual trade with the United States, and span sectors from wine to hockey equipment. President Donald Trump announced the 50 percent tariffs in an executive order on July 20, accusing Canada of "discriminatory treatment" in its trade policies. They were initially set to take effect on August 19 but Trump granted a three-day pause, saying the two countries were close to a deal.

"We were not prepared to compromise Canada's sovereignty or undermine our key industries," Carney said in a 22-minute address to Canadians. "You're at war when you're attacked, and we got attacked."

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said there are no future talks planned with Canada and that Washington is moving forward with measures to respond to Canadian retaliation. The breakdown complicates the future of the USMCA free trade deal.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford, whose province is hit hardest by the tariffs, said he backed Carney's position "tariff for tariff, dollar for dollar."

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said there are no future talks planned with Canada and that Washington is moving forward with measures to respond to Canadian retaliation. The breakdown complicates the future of the USMCA free trade deal.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford, whose province is hit hardest by the tariffs, said he backed Carney's position "tariff for tariff, dollar for dollar."

<article>
US 50% tariffs on Canadian goods take effect; Carney vows retaliation

OTTAWA (Reuters) — Canada will impose tariffs on US goods in retaliation for the 50 percent levies that took effect just after midnight on Saturday, Prime Minister Mark Carney said, after three days of trade talks between the two neighbours collapsed.

The "dollar for dollar" tariffs on imports of US steel, dairy, household appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics will take effect on September 8, the Tuesday after Labor Day.

The new US tariffs cover roughly $20 billion of Canadian exports, about 5 percent of Canada's annual trade with the United States, and span sectors from wine to hockey equipment. They were ordered under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 and stack on top of a 10 percent levy imposed earlier this month.

President Donald Trump announced the 50 percent tariffs in an executive order on July 20, accusing Canada of "discriminatory treatment" in its trade policies. They were initially set to take effect on August 19 but Trump granted a three-day pause, saying the two countries were close to a deal.

The pause ran out without an agreement. Late on Friday, Carney said he was suspending trade negotiations and ordering Canadian negotiators back to Ottawa.

"We were not prepared to compromise Canada's sovereignty or undermine our key industries," Carney said in a 22-minute address to Canadians. "You're at war when you're attacked, and we got attacked."

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said there are no future talks planned with Canada and that Washington is moving forward with measures to respond to Canadian retaliation. The breakdown complicates the future of the USMCA free trade deal.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford, whose province is hit hardest by the tariffs, said he backed Carney's position "tariff for tariff, dollar for dollar."
</article>

<article>
US 50% tariffs on Canadian goods take effect; Carney vows retaliation

OTTAWA (Reuters) — Canada will impose tariffs on US goods in retaliation for the 50 percent levies that took effect just after midnight on Saturday, Prime Minister Mark Carney said, after three days of trade talks between the two neighbours collapsed.

The "dollar for dollar" tariffs on imports of US steel, dairy, household appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics will take effect on September 8, the Tuesday after Labor Day.

The new US tariffs cover roughly $20 billion of Canadian exports, about 5 percent of Canada's annual trade with the United States, and span sectors from wine to hockey equipment. They were ordered under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 and stack on top of a 10 percent levy imposed earlier this month.

President Donald Trump announced the 50 percent tariffs in an executive order on July 20, accusing Canada of "discriminatory treatment" in its trade policies. They were initially set to take effect on August 19 but Trump granted a three-day pause, saying the two countries were close to a deal.

The pause ran out without an agreement. Late on Friday, Carney said he was suspending trade negotiations and ordering Canadian negotiators back to Ottawa.

"We were not prepared to compromise Canada's sovereignty or undermine our key industries," Carney said in a 22-minute address to Canadians. "You're at war when you're attacked, and we got attacked."

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said there are no future talks planned with Canada and that Washington is moving forward with measures to respond to Canadian retaliation. The breakdown complicates the future of the USMCA free trade deal.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford, whose province is hit hardest by the tariffs, said he backed Carney's position "tariff for tariff, dollar for dollar."

US 50% tariffs on Canadian goods take effect; Carney vows retaliation

OTTAWA (Reuters) — Canada will impose tariffs on US goods in retaliation for the 50 percent levies that took effect just after midnight on Saturday, Prime Minister Mark Carney said, after three days of trade talks between the two neighbours collapsed.

The "dollar for dollar" tariffs on imports of US steel, dairy, household appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics will take effect on September 8, the Tuesday after Labor Day.

The new US tariffs cover roughly $20 billion of Canadian exports, about 5 percent of Canada's annual trade with the United States, and span sectors from wine to hockey equipment. They were ordered under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 and stack on top of a 10 percent levy imposed earlier this month.

President Donald Trump announced the 50 percent tariffs in an executive order on July 20, accusing Canada of "discriminatory treatment" in its trade policies. They were initially set to take effect on August 19 but Trump granted a three-day pause, saying the two countries were close to a deal.

The pause ran out without an agreement. Late on Friday, Carney said he was suspending trade negotiations and ordering Canadian negotiators back to Ottawa.

"We were not prepared to compromise Canada's sovereignty or undermine our key industries," Carney said in a 22-minute address to Canadians. "You're at war when you're attacked, and we got attacked."

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said there are no future talks planned with Canada and that Washington is moving forward with measures to respond to Canadian retaliation. The breakdown complicates the future of the USMCA free trade deal.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford, whose province is hit hardest by the tariffs, said he backed Carney's position "tariff for tariff, dollar for dollar."

Evergrande founder Hui Ka Yan sentenced to life in prison

HONG KONG/SHENZHEN (Reuters) — The founder of China Evergrande Group, the world's most-indebted property developer, was sentenced to life in prison by a Chinese court on Thursday, five years after the firm's collapse shook the nation's economy and financial markets.

The Shenzhen Intermediate People's Court said it convicted 67-year-old Hui Ka Yan, also known as Xu Jiayin, of large-scale financial fraud in inflating the group's assets and concealing its liabilities, along with illegal fundraising and bribery. Hui, once Forbes Asia's richest man, pleaded guilty in April to eight charges.

The court ordered the confiscation of all of Hui's personal property, with political rights revoked for life, and said restitution for victims takes priority over state fines and asset seizures.

Evergrande Group was fined 8.82 billion yuan ($1.31 billion) and Evergrande Real Estate Group, its major mainland subsidiary, was fined 7 billion yuan ($1.04 billion), a combined 15.82 billion yuan (about $2.35 billion).

Five other senior executives were sentenced to prison terms ranging from six to 18 years, and 56 people in total were sentenced in connection with the collapse, state media reported.

Hui was separately fined 47 million yuan and banned from China's securities markets for life by the China Securities Regulatory Commission in 2024 over inflating company financial results.

At its peak, Evergrande employed about 200,000 people, and its default in 2021 triggered a property crisis that spread across the industry.

Evergrande founder Hui Ka Yan sentenced to life in prison

HONG KONG/SHENZHEN (Reuters) — The founder of China Evergrande Group, the world's most-indebted property developer, was sentenced to life in prison by a Chinese court on Thursday, five years after the firm's collapse shook the nation's economy and financial markets.

The Shenzhen Intermediate People's Court said it convicted 67-year-old Hui Ka Yan, also known as Xu Jiayin, of large-scale financial fraud in inflating the group's assets and concealing its liabilities, along with illegal fundraising and bribery. Hui, once Forbes Asia's richest man, pleaded guilty in April to eight charges.

The court ordered the confiscation of all of Hui's personal property, with political rights revoked for life, and said restitution for victims takes priority over state fines and asset seizures.

Evergrande Group was fined 8.82 billion yuan ($1.31 billion) and Evergrande Real Estate Group, its major mainland subsidiary, was fined 7 billion yuan ($1.04 billion), a combined 15.82 billion yuan (about $2.35 billion).

Five other senior executives were sentenced to prison terms ranging from six to 18 years, and 56 people in total were sentenced in connection with the collapse, state media reported.

Hui was separately fined 47 million yuan and banned from China's securities markets for life by the China Securities Regulatory Commission in 2024 over inflating company financial results.

At its peak, Evergrande employed about 200,000 people, and its default in 2021 triggered a property crisis that spread across the industry.

Hui was separately fined 47 million yuan and banned from China's securities markets for life by the China Securities Regulatory Commission in 2024 over inflating company financial results.

Hui was separately fined 47 million yuan and banned from China's securities markets for life by the China Securities Regulatory Commission in 2024 over inflating company financial results.

Hui was separately fined 47 million yuan and banned from China's securities markets for life by the China Securities Regulatory Commission in 2024 over inflating company financial results.

Hui was separately fined 47 million yuan and banned from China's securities markets for life by the China Securities Regulatory Commission in 2024 over inflating company financial results.

<article>
Evergrande founder Hui Ka Yan sentenced to life in prison

HONG KONG/SHENZHEN (Reuters) — The founder of China Evergrande Group, the world's most-indebted property developer, was sentenced to life in prison by a Chinese court on Thursday, five years after the firm's collapse shook the nation's economy and financial markets.

The Shenzhen Intermediate People's Court said it convicted 67-year-old Hui Ka Yan, also known as Xu Jiayin, of large-scale financial fraud in inflating the group's assets and concealing its liabilities, along with illegal fundraising and bribery. Hui, once Forbes Asia's richest man, pleaded guilty in April to eight charges.

The court ordered the confiscation of all of Hui's personal property, with political rights revoked for life, and said restitution for victims takes priority over state fines and asset seizures.

Evergrande Group was fined 8.82 billion yuan ($1.31 billion) and Evergrande Real Estate Group, its major mainland subsidiary, was fined 7 billion yuan ($1.04 billion), a combined 15.82 billion yuan (about $2.35 billion).

Five other senior executives were sentenced to prison terms ranging from six to 18 years, and 56 people in total were sentenced in connection with the collapse, state media reported.

Hui was separately fined 47 million yuan and banned from China's securities markets for life by the China Securities Regulatory Commission in 2024 over inflating company financial results.

At its peak, Evergrande employed about 200,000 people, and its default in 2021 triggered a property crisis that spread across the industry.

Gang attack near Port-au-Prince leaves 47 dead, 50 kidnapped

PORT-AU-PRINCE (AP) — At least 47 people were killed and more than 50 others kidnapped after armed men attacked a once-peaceful community near Haiti's capital earlier this week, the United Nations said Tuesday.

A powerful gang coalition raided the hillside community of Kenscoff, in the hills above Port-au-Prince, late on Sunday, setting fire to homes and killing residents, according to Kenscoff Mayor Jean Massillon, who called it a night of terror.

U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres condemned the attack, noting that 22 of the victims were reportedly executed in a church compound where displaced people had sought shelter. At least five of the 47 people killed were children, the U.N. Integrated Office in Haiti said.

It is believed to be one of the largest mass kidnappings in Haiti in recent years, and one gang leader is threatening to kill the hostages if authorities kill any gang members as they try to secure the community.

Gang members targeted a church and homes, including those owned by Dr. Jean "Bill" Pape, a renowned doctor who runs a non-governmental organization in Haiti that helps patients with HIV and tuberculosis. The mayor said two government employees were among the killed, including his cousin, who served as his security detail.

The mayor said members of Viv Ansanm, the gang coalition that the United States has designated as a foreign terrorist organization, also set fire to 25 homes.

Gang violence has displaced a record 1.5 million people across Haiti, where more than 3,050 people were reported killed from January to June, the U.N. said.

The mayor said members of Viv Ansanm, the gang coalition that the United States has designated as a foreign terrorist organization, also set fire to 25 homes.

The mayor said members of Viv Ansanm, the gang coalition that the United States has designated as a foreign terrorist organization, also set fire to 25 homes.

The mayor said members of Viv Ansanm, the gang coalition that the United States has designated as a foreign terrorist organization, also set fire to 25 homes.

The mayor said members of Viv Ansanm, the gang coalition that the United States has designated as a foreign terrorist organization, also set fire to 25 homes.

PORT-AU-PRINCE (AP) — At least 47 people were killed and more than 50 others kidnapped after armed men attacked a once-peaceful community near Haiti's capital earlier this week, the United Nations said Tuesday.

A powerful gang coalition raided the hillside community of Kenscoff, in the hills above Port-au-Prince, late on Sunday, setting fire to homes and killing residents, according to Kenscoff Mayor Jean Massillon, who called it a night of terror.

The mayor said two government employees were among the killed, including his cousin, who served as his security detail.

The mayor said members of Viv Ansanm, the gang coalition that the United States has designated as a foreign terrorist organization, also set fire to 25 homes.

Gang violence has displaced a record 1.5 million people across Haiti, where more than 3,050 people were reported killed from January to June, the U.N. said.

Opposition figure Juan Pablo Guanipa welcomed the releases but demanded that all political prisoners be freed "without exception, without delay, and promptly," saying each person returning home is "an immense relief" for families who have "suffered too much."

CARACAS (AFP) — Venezuela says it has freed 131 people considered political prisoners, in a sign of progress for national reconciliation following the United States' removal of former President Nicolas Maduro.

Those released had been granted "alternative measures from incarceration" under the Program for Peace and Democratic Coexistence, the country's interim government said on Friday, in a statement distributed by communications minister Miguel Perez Pirela. The releases took place at El Rodeo I prison in Guatire, in the Miranda state.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the release of more than 130 political prisoners was "a crucial step for the nation's reconciliation process." Since the US overthrew and detained Maduro on January 3, 1,046 Venezuelans have been released, Rubio added.

The opposition movement Vente Venezuela said it had independently verified the release of 43 detainees as of 4:58 p.m. local time and that it was continuing to review individual cases. The Foro Penal rights group confirmed the release of at least 40 political prisoners.

As of Monday, Foro Penal said 391 political prisoners remained behind bars.

Opposition figure Juan Pablo Guanipa welcomed the releases but demanded that all political prisoners be freed "without exception, without delay, and promptly," saying each person returning home is "an immense relief" for families who have "suffered too much."

CARACAS (AFP) — Venezuela says it has freed 131 people considered political prisoners, in a sign of progress for national reconciliation following the United States' removal of former President Nicolas Maduro.

Those released had been granted "alternative measures from incarceration" under the Program for Peace and Democratic Coexistence, the country's interim government said on Friday, in a statement distributed by communications minister Miguel Perez Pirela. The releases took place at El Rodeo I prison in Guatire, in the Miranda state.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the release of more than 130 political prisoners was "a crucial step for the nation's reconciliation process." Since the US overthrew and detained Maduro on January 3, 1,046 Venezuelans have been released, Rubio added.

As of Monday, Foro Penal said 391 political prisoners remained behind bars.

Opposition figure Juan Pablo Guanipa welcomed the releases but demanded that all political prisoners be freed "without exception, without delay, and promptly," saying each person returning home is "an immense relief" for families who have "suffered too much."

Those released had been granted "alternative measures from incarceration" under the Program for Peace and Democratic Coexistence, the country's interim government said on Friday, in a statement distributed by communications minister Miguel Perez Pirela. The releases took place at El Rodeo I prison in Guatire, in the Miranda state.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the release of more than 130 political prisoners was "a crucial step for the nation's reconciliation process." Since the US overthrew and detained Maduro on January 3, 1,046 Venezuelans have been released, Rubio added.

The opposition movement Vente Venezuela said it had independently verified the release of 43 detainees as of 4:58 p.m. local time and that it was continuing to review individual cases. The Foro Penal rights group confirmed the release of at least 40 political prisoners.

As of Monday, Foro Penal said 391 political prisoners remained behind bars.

Opposition figure Juan Pablo Guanipa welcomed the releases but demanded that all political prisoners be freed "without exception, without delay, and promptly," saying each person returning home is "an immense relief" for families who have "suffered too much."
